Bureaucratic priests come into power and add morality and messaging control over the people and the king. The major message is that the king must serve the people, with priests controlling the king. However, different bureaucratic factions will fight each other, leading to conflicting stories.

So, as bureaucratic priests take power, morality and messaging change accordingly. The king must learn humility, which is crucial to understand; otherwise, you can't grasp the Bible or similar texts.

To illustrate this process, let's consider three universities: Ohio State University, Connecticut College, and Middleberry. At each university, a significant event captured student imagination and was passed down through oral tradition, becoming increasingly exaggerated over time.

At Ohio State University, Michael James gets drunk before exams but still scores high. The story evolves to say he scores 100 on every exam while drunk. Naturally, it becomes even more exaggerated: Michael James bets his professor he can get 100 while intoxicated and succeeds.

After the exam, James bombs in front of the professor but still maintains his perfect score. This example naturally leads to storytelling exaggerations.

At Connecticut College, a football player scores a winning touchdown, which is later exaggerated to hitting touchdowns in every game. The story continues to become more detailed: the player hits home runs and wins championships with each touchdown.

Finally, at Middleberry College, Pat Jack drives around taking random piss breaks. This becomes even more exaggerated: he travels to new cities daily, pissing on sleeping bears, running up trees without pants, and needing forest rangers for rescue.

These stories become funnier and more detailed over time, eventually consolidating into a single narrative. At Harvard, Pitbull James is legendary, rolling an impossible exam, hitting home runs with one arm, and even pissing on a sleeping bear to knock it down. These exaggerated tales are further shaped by bureaucratic control as different versions emerge: when he became a billionaire and gave all his wealth to Harvard, or when he found true love in the woods, emphasizing writers over athletes.

The bureaucrats then alter these stories for better control of people, leading to multiple narratives that serve their purposes.
